sections.title: Georgia law-pack sign-off
sections.intro: Each card is one statement of Georgia law the site may make, with the authority it rests on. Once you sign a statement, new content may rely on it and the site check measures every page against it. Until then we publish no new Georgia legal claim. Approve, or give the wording you want; a correction comes back to you once more before it counts. "Approve all" on a group is fine.

sections.title: Wording on the pedestrian pages, held for you

items.title: Walking along a highway

pairs.now: Use the sidewalk; otherwise walk on the left side facing traffic.
pairs.proposed: "Use a sidewalk when one is available, otherwise the shoulder, and walk on the left side facing traffic only where there is neither."

items.question: § 56-5-3160(b)–(c) puts the shoulder before the left-side rule. Is the proposed wording right?

items.title: Crosswalk yield duty
items.question: The page now quotes § 56-5-3130(a) in full, but its "critical elements" bullets and FAQ 0 still state the yield duty without the condition "when traffic-control signals are not in place or not in operation". Should we add that condition there?

items.title: The "notwithstanding" gloss
items.question: The page reads § 56-5-3230's "notwithstanding" as overriding every other provision. The statute says "notwithstanding other provisions of any local ordinance". Should the gloss be narrowed to local ordinances?

items.title: Cyclists' equal rights
items.question: Two cycling pages (posts 4172, 4173) cite § 56-5-3435 for cyclists having the same rights as drivers. We've only verified that section for the passing distance. Is it the right cite for equal rights? If not, which section is?

items.title: Guilty pleas as evidence
items.question: Pages citing § 56-5-6160 carve out guilty pleas from the bar on using traffic convictions as evidence, relying on Samuel v. Mouzon. Is that right?

items.title: Troubled-teen FAQ: general deadline wording (live since 10-24)

pairs.now: A claim that abuse survivors generally get extended deadlines.
pairs.proposed: "It may not be too late, but some claims may already have expired. Filing deadlines depend on the kind of claim and the state where it is filed, and they are strict."

items.question: Is the general wording acceptable until the two deadlines above are signed?

items.title: Crosswalk yield duty: the no-signal condition

pairs.now: The duty to yield applies at both marked and unmarked crosswalks
pairs.proposed: Where traffic-control signals are not in place or not in operation, the duty to yield applies at both marked and unmarked crosswalks

pairs.now: Yes. S.C. Code § 56-5-3130 requires drivers to yield the right of way to pedestrians within any marked crosswalk or any unmarked crosswalk at an intersection.
pairs.proposed: Yes, where no traffic signal is in place or working. S.C. Code § 56-5-3130(a) then requires drivers to yield the right of way to pedestrians within any marked crosswalk or any unmarked crosswalk at an intersection.

pairs.now: The word "notwithstanding" is key — it means this duty applies regardless of any other provision, including situations where the pedestrian does not have the right of way.
pairs.proposed: The opening words, "notwithstanding other provisions of any local ordinance," mean no local ordinance can lower this duty. The duty also applies when the pedestrian does not have the right of way.

pairs.now: S.C. Code § 56-5-3435 grants cyclists the same rights as vehicle drivers and prohibits drivers from making turns across a cyclist's path unless the turn can be made safely.
pairs.proposed: S.C. Code § 56-5-3420 gives cyclists the same rights and duties as drivers, subject to statutory exceptions, and § 56-5-3435 requires a driver passing a cyclist to keep a safe operating distance.

pairs.now: FAQ: … South Carolina (S.C. Code § 56-5-3435) grant cyclists the same rights and duties as motor vehicle drivers.
pairs.proposed: FAQ: … South Carolina (S.C. Code § 56-5-3420) grant cyclists the same rights and duties as motor vehicle drivers.

pairs.now: S.C. Code § 56-5-3435 grants cyclists identical rights and duties as motor vehicle operators, including the right of way at intersections when traveling with a green signal or stop-sign priority.
pairs.proposed: S.C. Code § 56-5-3420 gives cyclists the same rights and duties as drivers, subject to statutory exceptions, so the ordinary right-of-way rules at intersections apply to them.

pairs.now: FAQ: … South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 56-5-3435), cyclists may use the full lane …
pairs.proposed: FAQ: … South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 56-5-3420), cyclists may use the full lane …

pairs.now: When reconstruction evidence or the driver's guilty plea proves the other driver was traveling at extreme speed …
pairs.proposed: When reconstruction evidence or the driver's guilty plea shows the other driver was traveling at extreme speed …

pairs.now: South Carolina gives injured workers more flexibility in choosing their treating physician than Georgia. You can typically select your own doctor, though the insurer can request a change under certain circumstances (S.C. Code § 42-15-60).
pairs.proposed: In South Carolina the employer may choose and furnish the treating physician, and the injured worker must accept that physician (S.C. Code § 42-15-60).

pairs.now: Unlike Georgia, South Carolina gives injured workers more flexibility in choosing their own treating physician (S.C. Code § 42-15-60)
pairs.proposed: The employer may choose and furnish the treating physician (S.C. Code § 42-15-60)
